plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a single planar point set with its convex hull traced as a thick gray polygon. Five hull vertices appear as filled black dots and are labeled p_0 at the bottom left, p_1 at the lower right, p_2 at the right, p_3 at the top, and p_4 at the left; eight further black dots lie scattered inside the polygon, joined to nothing. A dashed straight line passes through p_0 and continues upward through p_3; at both of those vertices a pair of short arrows straddles the dashed line, reading left chain with an arrow pointing left and right chain with an arrow pointing right. Every hull vertex also carries a short vertical tick and a horizontal reference ray: at p_0, p_1, and p_2 the ray points right, and a thin arc sweeps from it around to the next hull edge, the arc at p_0 being very narrow and the one at p_2 close to a half turn. At p_4 and p_3 the ray points left instead, with arcs swept from it the same way. The arcs are the quantities being compared, since the next vertex along the boundary is the one subtending the smallest such angle. The picture lays out the wrapping order in which hull vertices are discovered, first up the right chain to the highest point and then back down the left.

interactionPlan.concept: Jarvis's march constructs a convex hull by repeatedly sweeping a ray from the current vertex to find the point with the smallest polar angle, splitting the process into a right chain and a left chain.
elements: 5 hull vertices shown as black dots, labeled p0 (bottom), p1 (bottom-right), p2 (far right), p3 (top), and p4 (far left)
8 interior points shown as black dots, scattered inside the polygon boundary
Thick gray polygon edges connecting p0-p1-p2-p3-p4-p0 to form the convex hull
A dashed dividing line passing through p0 and p3, extending slightly past them
Text labels 'left chain' and 'right chain' with small horizontal arrows pointing left and right, located at the top (near p3) and bottom (near p0)
Short vertical tick marks intersecting each of the 5 hull vertices
Horizontal reference rays originating from each hull vertex (pointing right for p0, p1, p2; pointing left for p3, p4)
Thin circular arcs at each hull vertex, sweeping from the horizontal reference ray to the outgoing hull edge

interactions.label: Construction Phase
interactions.teaches: Switching chains flips the horizontal reference ray from right-facing to left-facing, allowing the minimum-angle logic to work seamlessly for both sides of the hull.

interactions.label: Algorithm Step
interactions.teaches: Advancing the state moves the active vertex and highlights the minimum-angle sweep to the next hull edge.
Hovering over any interior point draws a dashed ray and its corresponding angle from the active vertex, proving visually that its angle is larger than the one chosen for the actual hull edge.

demo_steps.title: Starting the right chain
demo_steps.narration: Jarvis's march begins at the lowest point, p0. Using a rightward-pointing horizontal ray as a baseline, it finds the point p1 with the smallest polar angle.

demo_steps.title: Reaching the top
demo_steps.narration: The process repeats, finding p2 and then p3. Because p3 is the highest point in the set, the right chain is complete.

demo_steps.title: Flipping directions
demo_steps.narration: To travel down the left side, the reference ray flips to point left. The algorithm again seeks the smallest polar angle, which now discovers p4.

demo_steps.title: Closing the hull
demo_steps.narration: The left chain continues until it hits the starting point p0. The boundary is now closed.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: By splitting the boundary into two chains and flipping the reference axis at the extremes, Jarvis's march only ever needs to compute and compare angles between 0 and 180 degrees.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Layout 13 points total. The hull points are p0 (bottom left-ish), p1 (bottom right), p2 (far right), p3 (top, slightly right of p0), p4 (far left). Draw the hull with a thick gray stroke. The dashed line separating the chains passes exactly through p0 and p3. The arcs must originate exactly on the horizontal rays and sweep to the gray edges. Ensure p0, p1, p2 have right-pointing arrows for their reference rays, and p3, p4 have left-pointing arrows. The arcs at p0 and p4 are visually small (acute angles), while p2 is almost 180 degrees (obtuse angle).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button for stepping through Jarvis's march from p0 to p4: the active reference ray, angle sweep, and next hull edge light up at each vertex, making clear how the smallest polar angle chooses the next boundary point.
- Toggle between right-chain and left-chain construction: the horizontal reference direction flips at the highest and lowest points and the active half of the hull is emphasized, making clear why the wrapping rule changes direction across the two chains.
- Hover for any interior point during a step: its candidate angle appears beside the chosen hull angle, making clear why interior points are skipped even though they are in the same point set.

authoredContext:
Jarvis’s march computes the convex hull of a set Q of points by a technique known as package wrapping (or gift wrapping). The algorithm runs in time O.nh/, where h is the number of vertices of CH.Q/. When h is o.lg n/, Jarvis’s march is asymptotically faster than Graham’s scan. Intuitively, Jarvis’s march simulates wrapping a taut piece of paper around the set Q. We start by taping the end of the paper to the lowest point in the set, that is, to the same point p0 with which we start Graham’s scan. We know that this point must be a vertex of the convex hull. We pull the paper to the right to make it taut, and then we pull it higher until it touches a point. This point must also be a vertex of the convex hull. Keeping the paper taut, we continue in this way around the set of vertices until we come back to our original point p0. More formally, Jarvis’s march builds a sequence H D hp0; p1; : : : ; ph1i of the vertices of CH.Q/. We start with p0. As Figure 33.9 shows, the next vertex p1 in the convex hull has the smallest polar angle with respect to p0. (In case of ties, we choose the point farthest from p0.) Similarly, p2 has the smallest polar angle with respect to p1, and so on. When we reach the highest vertex, say pk (breaking
ties by choosing the farthest such vertex), we have constructed, as Figure 33.9
shows, the right chain of CH.Q/. To construct the left chain, we start at pk and
choose pkC1 as the point with the smallest polar angle with respect to pk, but from
the negative x-axis. We continue on, forming the left chain by taking polar angles
from the negative x-axis, until we come back to our original vertex p0.
We could implement Jarvis’s march in one conceptual sweep around the convex
hull, that is, without separately constructing the right and left chains. Such implementations typically keep track of the angle of the last convex-hull side chosen and
require the sequence of angles of hull sides to be strictly increasing (in the range
of 0 to 2_x0019_ radians). The advantage of constructing separate chains is that we need
not explicitly compute angles; the techniques of Section 33.1 suffice to compare
angles.
If implemented properly, Jarvis’s march has a running time of O.nh/. For each
of the h vertices of CH.Q/, we find the vertex with the minimum polar angle. Each
comparison between polar angles takes O.1/ time, using the techniques of Section 33.1. As Section 9.1 shows, we can compute the minimum of n values in O.n/
time if each comparison takes O.1/ time. Thus, Jarvis’s march takes O.nh/ time.
